:::{#rem-integrable-integral}
#### Riemann integrable functions and Riemann integrals

A bounded function $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$
exactly when its Riemann integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
(@def-riemann-integral) exists;
the integral is the common limit of the sums.
For example, let $g(x) = 1$ when $x$ is [rational](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/number-systems.html#def-rational-numbers)
and $g(x) = 0$ when $x$ is [irrational](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/number-systems.html#def-irrational-numbers),
on $[0, 1]$.
Every subinterval contains both rational and irrational points.
Choosing every sample point rational gives
$\sumin 1 \cd \change x_i = 1$
for every partition,
because the widths $\change x_i$ add up to the length $1 - 0 = 1$ of $[0, 1]$,
and choosing every sample point irrational gives
$\sumin 0 \cd \change x_i = 0$.
The two limits differ,
so $g$ is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$,
and $\int_0^1 g(x)\,dx$ does not exist.

:::
